01 · Intro

An Example to Keep in Mind

Throughout, the physical notion of center of mass is a good source of intuition.

Example

A massless beam lies along the interval \([1,6]\). Six point masses are attached:

  • \(m_1=0.10\) kg at \(x=1\)
  • \(m_2=0.30\) kg at \(x=2\)
  • \(m_3=0.05\) kg at \(x=3\)
  • \(m_4=0.40\) kg at \(x=4\)
  • \(m_5=0.10\) kg at \(x=5\)
  • \(m_6=0.05\) kg at \(x=6\)

Where is the center of mass located along the beam?

Solution

The center of mass is located at \(\overline{x}\), the (weighted) average of the locations of the masses:

\[\overline{x}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^6x_im_i}{m_{tot}} =\frac{(1)(0.1)+(2)(0.3)+(3)(0.05)+(4)(0.4)+(5)(0.1)+(6)(0.05)}{1}=\boxed{3.25}\]

03 · A Roll of the Dice

Center of Mass \(\iff\) Expected Value

Take away the static scenario of masses on a beam and instead look at a simple game of chance.

Example

We roll an unfair 6-sided die with the following weights (likelihoods):

  • \(p_1=0.10\) of rolling \(x=1\)
  • \(p_2=0.30\) of rolling \(x=2\)
  • \(p_3=0.05\) of rolling \(x=3\)
  • \(p_4=0.40\) of rolling \(x=4\)
  • \(p_5=0.10\) of rolling \(x=5\)
  • \(p_6=0.05\) of rolling \(x=6\)

If \(X\) is the (random) outcome of a single roll, what is the expected value of \(X\)?

Solution

The expected value is the average of the possible outcomes weighted according to their respective probabilities: \[E[X]=\sum_{i=1}^6x_ip_i=\boxed{3.25}\]

05 · What Does “Expected” Mean?

Why Is It Called the Expected Value?

The expected value is the theoretical average outcome of a random experiment over many repetitions.

The average of a finite sample

Suppose we roll the die \(N\) times, obtaining outcomes \(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_N\). Their sample mean is

\[ \overline X_N =\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}. \]

This average depends on the rolls we actually observe, so it can vary from one experiment to another.

The theoretical expectation

The expected value \(E[X]\) is determined by the probabilities of the possible outcomes, not by any particular set of rolls. As we repeat the experiment more and more times, the sample mean tends toward the expected value:

\[ \boxed{\overline X_N\longrightarrow E[X]} \qquad\text{as }N\to\infty. \]

For our loaded die, \(E[X]=3.25\). A finite sample might average \(3.1\) or \(3.6\), but over many rolls its average should settle near \(3.25\).

Important: Expected value does not necessarily mean the outcome you are most likely to get. It describes the long-run average, not the most likely individual result.

06 · Great Expectations

Expected Value of a Function with Discrete Outputs

Example

Suppose it costs $3 to play a game: roll the same loaded die as before and receive a dollar amount equal to the number rolled. What is the expected net profit? (Hint: still a weighted average...but of what?)

Solution

From outcome to payoff

Let \(X\) be the number rolled. The net profit is \(g(X)=X-3\):

\[ \begin{array}{c|rrrrrr} X & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6\\ \hline g(X) & -2 & -1 & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 \end{array} \]

We take the probability-weighted average of the possible payoffs:

\[ \begin{aligned} E[g(X)] &=\sum_{i=1}^6g(i)P(X=i)\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^6(i-3)P(X=i)\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^6iP(X=i) -3\sum_{i=1}^6P(X=i)\\ &=E[X]-3\\ &=3.25-3=\$0.25. \end{aligned} \]

Interpretation: The expected net profit is 25 cents per game.

Key idea: To find the expected value of a function of a random outcome, apply the function to each possible outcome, then take the probability-weighted average.

07 · Discrete → Continuous

From Weighted Sums to Weighted Integrals

For a discrete random variable, we calculate the expected value by taking a probability-weighted average:

\[ E[X]=\sum_i x_iP(X=x_i). \]

Now imagine that our random outcome is a point \((X,Y)\) in a region \(D\subset\mathbb R^2\). There are infinitely many possible outcomes. How can we take their weighted average?

Idea: approximate the region by small cells

Partition \(D\) into tiny cells \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\). Choose a representative point \((x_i,y_i)\) in each cell.

Treat each cell as one possible outcome: if \(X\) lands in \(A_i\), its coordinates are approximately \((x_i,y_i)\).

The expected \(x\)-coordinate is then approximated by the discrete weighted average

\[ E[X]\approx\sum_i x_iP((X,Y)\in A_i). \]

For a probability density function \(f\), the probability of landing in a sufficiently small cell is approximately its density at that point times the cell's area:

\[ P((X,Y)\in A_i)\approx f(x_i,y_i)\,\Delta A_i. \]

Substituting gives

\[ E[X]\approx\sum_i x_i f(x_i,y_i)\,\Delta A_i. \]

As the cells get smaller, this Riemann sum becomes a double integral:

\[ \boxed{E[X]=\iint_D x f(x,y)\,dA.} \]

Takeaway: The integral is still a weighted average. We have replaced a discrete collection of outcomes, each with an associated finite amount of probability mass \(P(X=x_i)\), by probability density \(f\) times infinitesimal area \(dA\).

08 · The Continuous Setting

A Random Experiment with Outcomes in \(\mathbb{R}^2\)

Example

We throw darts at a circular board \(D=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\leq16\}\). The location \((X,Y)\) of each throw follows the probability density

\[ f(x,y)=\frac{25-x^2-(y-1)^2}{256\pi}. \]

For any region \(C\subseteq D\), the probability of landing in \(C\) is

\[ P((X,Y)\in C)=\iint_C f(x,y)\,dA. \]

Use this to answer the following questions:

  1. What is the probability of hitting the board within 1 unit of its boundary?
  2. What are the expected \(x\)- and \(y\)-coordinates of a throw?
Solution
  1. The outer ring is \(R=\{(x,y):9\leq x^2+y^2\leq16\}\). Thus, \[ P((X,Y)\in R)=\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA. \]

    In polar coordinates, this becomes

    \[ \begin{aligned} P((X,Y)\in R) &=\frac{1}{256\pi} \int_0^{2\pi}\int_3^4 (24-r^2+2r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta\\ &=\frac{1}{128}\int_3^4(24-r^2)r\,dr\\ &=\boxed{\frac{161}{512}\approx0.31}. \end{aligned} \]
  2. Imagine \(f(x,y)\) represents the density of a two-dimensional sheet covering \(D\). The expected coordinates are the coordinates of its center of mass. \[ E[X]=\iint_D xf(x,y)\,dA =\frac{1}{256\pi}\iint_D x(25-x^2-(y-1)^2)\,dA. \] Using polar coordinates, \[ \begin{aligned} E[X] &=\frac{1}{256\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^4 r\cos\theta(24-r^2+2r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta\\ &=\boxed{0}. \end{aligned} \] Similarly, \[ \begin{aligned} E[Y] &=\frac{1}{256\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^4 r\sin\theta(24-r^2+2r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta\\ &=\boxed{\frac12}. \end{aligned} \]

    Intuition: The density is symmetric in \(x\), so the mass balances across the \(y\)-axis and \(E[X]=0\). The density is shifted upward, giving \(E[Y]>0\).

09 · Is It Worth It?

Expected Payout

Still throwing darts at the same board with same distribution, but now there are high stakes.

Example

Each throw costs \$1. If we hit the bullseye \(B = \{(x,y)\,:\,x^2+y^2\leq 1\},\) we win \$5; if we hit anywhere else in \(D\), we win nothing.

  • Write our profit for a single throw as a function \(g(x,y)\) depending on the coordinates \((x,y)\) of where the dart lands.
  • What is \(E[g(x,y)]\)? Explain.

    • Solution

  • Our profit is \$4 if \((x,y)\) is in \(B\), -\$1 otherwise. Thus \[g(x,y)=\begin{cases}4,\;\;(x,y)\;\text{in}\;\;B\\ -1,\;\;\text{otherwise}\end{cases}.\]
  • \(E[g(x,y)]\) is the expected profit from a single dart throw. Mathematically, \[E[g(x,y)]=\iint_D g(x,y)f(x,y)\,dA=\iint_B 4f(x,y)\,dA + \iint_{D\setminus B} (-1)f(x,y)\,dA\] \[=\frac{4}{256\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^1 (-r^2+2r\sin\theta+24)r\,dr\,d\theta -\frac{1}{256\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_1^4(-r^2+2r\sin\theta+24)r\,dr\,d\theta\] \[\ldots = -\frac{277}{512}\approx \boxed{-0.54}\] Takeaway: We expect to lose money playing this game!

    • 09
    10 · Well, in summary...

    From Center of Mass to Probability

    1. Expected value is a weighted average.

    For a discrete random variable, \[ E[X]=\sum_i x_iP(X=x_i). \]

    2. Density distributes probability across a region.

    A probability density satisfies \[ \iint_D f(x,y)\,dA=1, \] and for \(C\subseteq D\), \[ P((X,Y)\in C)=\iint_C f(x,y)\,dA. \]

    3. Double integrals give continuous expectations.

    \[ E[g(X,Y)]=\iint_D g(x,y)f(x,y)\,dA. \] Choosing \(g(x,y)=x\) or \(g(x,y)=y\) gives the expected coordinates.

    4. Expected value describes a long-run average.

    Individual outcomes vary, but the sample mean approaches the theoretical expectation over many independent repetitions.

    One unifying idea: Probability, expected value, and expected payoff all come from weighted averages according to the likelihood of occurrence. Sums are used in the discrete setting and integrals in the continuous setting.
